newsitem.title: THAILAND: Peregrine sees sharp fall in Thai economic growth.
newsitem.headline: Peregrine sees sharp fall in Thai economic growth.

text.p: Peregrine Fixed Income Ltd (PFIL) forecast on Tuesday that Thailand's gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 1996 would fall sharply to 6.2 percent from 8.5 percent.

"This rate is far lower than the central bank's forecast of 7.8 percent and well below present market expectations," PFIL's Singapore-based market research director, David Carbon, said in his latest report, received here.
"It will also mark Thailand's smallest expansion since 1987 when the economy grew 4.9 perecent," PFIL said in the report.
"Thailand's high-flying economy has lost an engine. It is a short hop from slow industrial production growth to slow GDP growth overall," the report said.
"Although 6.0 percent should provide a firm floor, the risk to the forecast is that growth could be slower still," it said.

Thailand's robust economy has grown at an averaged rate of 9.8 percent a year since 1987. But this year it has begun to slow down, affected by sluggish exports and industrial production growth as well as private investment.

Thai economic growth could even falter to 5.0 percent or more if export growth continued to slow more sharply than anticipated or if the performance of the financial sector, which accounted for about 8.0 percent of GDP, ran into trouble, PFIL said.
The Bank of Thailand recently scaled down to 10.2 percent its 1996 export growth target from a 17.4 percent growth projection set earlier this year.
In the first seven months of this year, Thailand said its export growth was at a meagre 3.8 percent against 26.2 percent in the same period a year ago.
PFIL acknowledged that export growth has fallen throughout most of Southeast Asia, with the notable exception of Indonesia, but said it had dropped more severely in Thailand than elsewhere.
Thailand's export growth slowdown was a cyclical problem and not a structural one affected also by a slowdown in global demand for certain products, it added.
PFIL said industrial production growth for 1996 was projected to drop to 6.5 percent from 11.95 percent in 1995, the slowest growth rate since 1986.
Agricultural production would not pick up the slack from other key sectors given current rising food prices.
